title: CORS
body:
*Cross origin resource sharing*
Javascript is *filled* with security threats.

One way to try to limit these security threats is to not allow different domains to execute.
Unfortunately,  by default the browser considers JSON from a different domain to be *not allowed*. That is, unless explicitely allowed by CORS policy settings, we can't fetch 3rd party APIs. D: 

So why can we use Randy's [[API]]s?
Because in his http headers, he has
`Access-Control-Allow-Origin:*` Which basically gives access to anyone for teaching purposes, generally you shouldn't do this. 


---

The thing to be clear about: **CORS is enforced by the browser, not by the server.** The
request is usually sent and the server usually answers it. What the browser does is refuse to
hand the response to your JavaScript unless the `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` header says the
[[Origin]] it came from is allowed. `curl` and a [[Node.js]] server ignore the whole mechanism,
because neither is a browser protecting a logged-in user.

That is also why it is not a defence for the server. CORS exists to stop *a page you did not
write* from reading *your* data using the user's cookies; it does nothing about someone
calling the API directly. See [[Same-Origin Policy]], which is the rule CORS relaxes.

Anything past a plain GET (a custom header, a JSON `Content-Type`, a PUT or DELETE) makes the
browser send an OPTIONS [[Preflight Request]] first and wait for permission before sending the
real one. Randy's `Access-Control-Allow-Origin:*` skips all of it by allowing everyone, which
is correct for a public teaching API and wrong for anything with a session behind it, because
`*` cannot be combined with credentials at all.
